article.overview: A sample drill is a powered tool that penetrates the lunar regolith (the loose layer of dust, soil and rock fragments that covers the Moon's surface) and removes a cylindrical core. A scoop collects material from the top few centimetres. A drill can recover material from depth, which allows scientists to examine how the regolith changes with depth and how it has been layered by impacts and other processes. Four generations of lunar drilling hardware are documented in public sources: Soviet automatic drills on Luna 16 (1970), Luna 20 (1972) and Luna 24 (1976); the astronaut-operated Apollo Lunar Surface Drill on Apollo 15, 16 and 17 (1971-1972); robotic coring drills on China's Chang'e-5 (2020) and Chang'e-6 (2024) sample-return missions; and NASA's TRIDENT drill, flown on the Intuitive Machines IM-2 lander in 2025. TRIDENT powered on and completed its commanded motions, but the lander came to rest on its side and no drilling test into the surface was reported. No single design defines a sample drill. The examples differ in size, power source, depth capability and sample handling, and should not be compared directly.
article.description: A lunar sample drill generally has a drive unit (motor, gearbox and, in some designs, a percussion mechanism), a coring bit, one or more hollow core stems or a core tube, and a means of retaining the core. Several designs also have a method for sealing or protecting the sample after extraction. The Apollo Lunar Surface Drill was a cordless, battery-operated motor with specialised bits and modular hollow core stems. Each core stem segment is about 40 cm long, and joined together they reached as deep as 10 ft (about 3 m). The Chang'e-5 coring drill used a rotary-percussive mechanism to take an intact core, which was delivered to the ascender in a Kevlar tube. TRIDENT (The Regolith and Ice Drill for Exploring New Terrain) is about 1 m long and uses rotary and percussive actuators. It was designed to stop at any depth commanded from the ground and to deposit its sample on the surface for analysis by the MSOLO mass spectrometer.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The main purpose of a sample drill is to obtain material from below the surface so that it can be studied in a laboratory or, for in-situ missions, analysed on the spot. Stratigraphy and depth profiles: a core preserves the order in which material was deposited. One Chang'e-5 study summary reports that grain size increases with depth in the drilled samples compared with a scooped sample; this summary was not opened in full and should be treated as provisional. Space weathering and solar-wind records: Chang'e-5 researchers describe the value of the drilled core of lunar soil for studying space weathering and the solar wind. Volatiles and ice prospecting: TRIDENT was built to investigate regolith and ice, and NASA describes its sample as analysed by MSOLO, which measures gases near the lander; no ice measurement was reported from the 2025 flight. Sample return: drilled cores returned to Earth are a source of material for laboratory analysis, including the Soviet Luna 24 core, which was reported at 160 cm long and 8 mm in diameter.
article.operating_principle: A sample drill generally combines two motions. Rotation turns the bit to cut and loosen material. Percussion (hammering) helps break up harder regolith or rock fragments and drive the bit into the ground. The Apollo drill was a battery-powered rotary-percussion drill operating at 280 rotations per minute and 2270 blows per minute, speeds low enough that cooling of the bit was not required. Its core stems were added one by one as the hole deepened, and the drill was then removed so the core string could be extracted. The Chang'e-5 drill used a rotary-percussive mechanism to recover a core into a flexible Kevlar tube that could be compacted for transfer. TRIDENT ran through a sequence of ground-commanded steps: releasing launch locks, extending its z-stages, rotating and percussing the auger, and running a core heater and temperature sensor. NASA reports that its actuators performed as designed and completed each commanded drilling stage. The mission did not produce a reported drilling depth or sample result.
article.scientific_importance: Drilled cores are one of the few ways to examine lunar material below the first few centimetres without relying only on surface observations. The Apollo deep cores, the Soviet cores from Luna 16, 20 and 24, and the Chang'e-5 and Chang'e-6 cores each provide different layers of information. The Apollo 15-17 deep cores allowed researchers to study the regolith to depths of metres rather than only the surface layer. The Luna 24 core was reported at 160 cm long, one of the deepest Soviet lunar cores. Chang'e-5 and Chang'e-6 returned samples from the near side and the far side respectively; Chang'e-6 returned the first samples from the Moon's far side. These results depend on careful documentation of depth, orientation and handling, because a core that is disturbed or mixed loses its stratigraphic value.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal mass, size or power requirement for a sample drill. The values below describe specific historical, flown or reported instruments and should not be generalised.

examples.name: Apollo Lunar Surface Drill (Apollo 15, 16 and 17)
examples.flown_on: Apollo 15, 16 and 17 according to the Smithsonian record. The NASA Working on the Moon drilling page also lists Apollo 13 among the missions carrying the drill; the Apollo 13 mission did not land on the Moon, so lunar drilling is described only for Apollo 15-17.
examples.drilling_performance: Two holes were drilled to 3 m to emplace heat-flow probes, and a 2-3 m deep core was collected.
examples.museum_object_mass_note: 13.4 kg (29.5 lb) is the mass of the museum object as recorded (inventory A19750038000). It is not a verified flight mass for the complete surface package, which also included stems, a stem rack, a treadle and a wrench.
examples.operational_lessons: The drill operator experienced fatigue, the drill was often difficult to release from the top of the drill string, and a jack was added for extracting the Apollo 16 and 17 cores.

examples.name: Luna 16, Luna 20 and Luna 24 automatic drills
examples.type: Soviet robotic sample-return missions with automatic drilling
examples.luna_16_1970: Secondary sources report that the automatic drill stopped at 35 cm and returned about 101 g of soil. Not confirmed in a primary Soviet or NASA document during this research.
examples.luna_20_1972: Secondary sources conflict: one reports penetration of 250 mm and another a depth of a metre or more; reported sample masses are 30 g and 55 g. No reliable Luna 20 depth or mass is recorded.
examples.luna_24_1976: A NASA Lunar Science Conference paper describes a 160 cm core with a diameter of 8 mm that was drilled, extracted and returned to Earth. It does not separately state the drilling depth or the sample mass.
examples.core_record_note: A NASA technical record on Luna 16 and Luna 20 core material confirms that core samples from both missions were studied, but does not describe the drill or report depth or mass.

examples.name: Chang'e-5 coring drill
examples.type: Robotic coring drill on a lunar lander, with sample return
examples.achieved_depth: Several peer-reviewed analyses, reported through secondary summaries, state that the drill penetrated about 1 m, short of its planned 2 m. Most drilled samples came from 0-73.8 cm. The eoportal reference states that post-landing reports describe drilling to about 2 m. This conflict is recorded in limitations_and_uncertainties.
examples.core_handling: Core delivered to the ascender in a Kevlar tube. Samples were packed into a vacuum container inside the ascender, sealed with a high-vacuum sealing device, and transferred to the return capsule by a robotic system whose specifications were not disclosed.

sample_mass.target_breakdown: 0.5 kg from drilling and 1.5 kg from scooping

examples.drill_length_and_mass: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

examples.name: Chang'e-6 sampling (drill and scoop)
examples.type: Robotic sampling on the lunar far side combining a scoop and a drill
examples.mass_note: China's National Space Administration gave a preliminary total of 1,935.3 g, about 204 g more than Chang'e-5. The source does not separate drill and scoop contributions.
examples.drill_depth_target: Secondary reporting describes an original target of about 2 kg of samples from drilling up to 2 m. No primary CNSA specification for the drill was reviewed.
examples.drill_dimensions_and_power: Not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

examples.name: PRIME-1 TRIDENT drill (IM-2, 2025)
examples.type: NASA flight drill with commercial mass spectrometer, flown on the Intuitive Machines IM-2 lander
examples.drilling_mode: Rotary and percussive actuators; designed to stop at any commanded depth.
examples.operational_result: The drill powered on and completed each commanded stage, but the lander came to rest on its side in a crater and the mission ended after about 10 hours of operation.
examples.depth_goal_and_diameter: Not stated in the NASA article reviewed.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The examples differ substantially. The Apollo drill was an astronaut-operated, modular drill with separate stems and a cradle; the Chang'e-5 and Chang'e-6 drills were robotic coring systems integrated into landers; TRIDENT was about 1 m long and designed for commanded-depth drilling. Dimensions must always be tied to a named instrument and source. The Apollo museum object dimensions (58 x 24 x 12 cm overall, 16 x 15 x 46 cm motor) are not flight-configuration dimensions for the full surface package.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: Mass is reported only for specific instruments. The Apollo drill museum object is recorded at 13.4 kg (29.5 lb). Chang'e-5 returned 1,731 g of samples in total, and Chang'e-6 returned 1,935.3 g by CNSA's preliminary calculation. No verified mass is available for the drill alone on Chang'e-5, Chang'e-6 or TRIDENT in the sources reviewed.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Apollo drill: battery-powered (capacity not stated in sources reviewed). TRIDENT: power not quantified in the NASA article reviewed; it included a core heater and temperature sensor. Chang'e-5 and Chang'e-6 drill power: not publicly specified in the sources reviewed.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A sample drill must work in a vacuum, across large temperature swings and in abrasive dust. Thermal control: TRIDENT included a core heater and temperature sensor, used during the mission to monitor temperature change during drilling. Heating from drilling: the Apollo drill was operated at speeds low enough that the bit did not require cooling. Sample integrity: the Chang'e-5 sample container was designed for high-vacuum sealing to keep samples intact for return to Earth. Mechanical support: a drill string must be supported and stabilised; Apollo operators reported difficulty handling the drill and stems, and jacks were used to extract the Apollo 16 and 17 cores. Regolith variability: Chang'e-5 analyses report irregular high-density zones and a possible rock fragment that may have limited the depth reached; these are inferences from published analyses, not confirmed events.
article.limitations: Depth capability versus depth reached: design depth, planned depth and depth actually reached differ for Chang'e-5, and reported drilling depth varies between sources. Stratigraphic disturbance: a drill can mix or compact material, and the Apollo handling difficulties could affect how the core was extracted and recorded. Limited measured data for some payloads: Luna 20 depth and mass conflict between sources, Luna 16 values come from secondary sources, and the TRIDENT drilling depth was not reached in flight. No universal specification: values for the Apollo, Luna, Chang'e and TRIDENT examples describe different instruments and missions.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A sample drill is a surface payload. It is integrated with a lander or return system, delivered to the Moon, operated on the surface and, for sample-return missions, transferred into a return vehicle.
transportation_process: Earth integration and launch: each example was integrated into a spacecraft or lander; the TRIDENT drill was delivered to the lunar surface on IM-2.

Lunar transfer and landing: each example reached the Moon as part of a lander or spacecraft; the IM-2 lander touched down on 6 March 2025 about 400 m from its target at Mons Mouton, near the lunar south pole.

Deployment and operation: Apollo drilling was performed by astronauts using the drill package (stem rack, treadle and wrench); Chang'e-5 used a robotic arm and scoop together with the drill; TRIDENT was ground-commanded to extend its drill and run drilling steps.
Sample transfer: for Chang'e-5, the core was delivered to the ascender in a Kevlar tube, and the sample container was transferred to the return capsule by a robotic transfer system.
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Apollo: astronaut-operated, with modular stems added one at a time and a jack used for extraction on Apollo 16 and 17. Chang'e-5: robotic coring drill on the lander with core transfer to the ascender. TRIDENT: ground-commanded drill extension and drilling sequence after landing.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Apollo 15, 16 and 17 (astronaut deployment); Luna 16, 20 and 24 (automatic drilling); Chang'e-5 (2020) and Chang'e-6 (2024) robotic sampling; IM-2 with TRIDENT (2025).
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No compatibility with a specific lander, rover or spacecraft is asserted beyond the documented missions named above. A new sample drill would need verified mass, dimensions, mounting points, power, thermal and data interfaces before any compatibility assessment.

article.historical_significance: Luna 16, Luna 20 and Luna 24 (Soviet, 1970-1976): Soviet automatic missions returned drilled lunar soil cores without astronaut involvement. Apollo 15, 16 and 17 (1971-1972): astronauts used the Apollo Lunar Surface Drill to recover deep cores, providing a record of the regolith beyond the surface layer. Chang'e-5 (2020): China returned a drilled and scooped sample from the near side. Chang'e-6 (2024): China returned the first far-side samples, collected by drill and scoop. IM-2 and TRIDENT (2025): a commercial lander carried a NASA drill to the lunar south pole region; the drill completed its commanded motions, but the mission did not produce drilled samples.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Conflicting Chang'e-5 depth: secondary analyses report about 1 m reached, but the eoportal reference states that post-landing reports describe drilling to about 2 m. The primary Chang'e-5 mission report was not located, and the Remote Sensing paper (MDPI, 2022, 14, 3378) could not be opened (HTTP 403) and the International Journal of Robotics Research paper was cited only through a secondary summary. Unverified Chang'e-5 drilled mass: the 259.72 g figure comes from a secondary summary. Luna 20 conflicts: depth and mass values conflict and are not recorded as reliable. Luna 16 values: the 35 cm depth and 101 g mass come from secondary sources and were not confirmed in a primary document. Apollo 13 listing: the NASA Working on the Moon page lists Apollo 13 among drill flights, while the Smithsonian record lists Apollo 15-17; Apollo 13 did not land, so no Apollo 13 lunar drilling is described. TRIDENT results: no drilling depth, sample mass or ice measurement from the 2025 flight is in the sources reviewed; NASA said data analysis would continue. Chang'e-6 drill specifications rely on secondary reporting, and the CNSA preliminary total does not separate drill and scoop contributions. Images: no direct image asset URL for any drill was verified in this pass; the only image entry is a linked museum record.

Where a direct image asset URL could not be verified without a query string, image_url is null and the source page is retained. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery.

data_quality_notes: Chang'e-5 drilling depth conflicts: secondary analyses report about 1 m reached (planned 2 m; most samples from 0-73.8 cm), while the eoportal reference states post-landing reports describe drilling to about 2 m. Unresolved; primary CNSA mission report not located.
Chang'e-5 drilled-sample mass of 259.72 g comes from a secondary summary and is unverified; the total returned (1,731 g) is from eoportal.
Chang'e-5 Remote Sensing paper (MDPI 14, 3378) returned HTTP 403 and was not opened; statements attributed to it come from search summaries.

Chinese Journal of Aeronautics and Icarus Chang'e-5 studies were accessed only through secondary summary pages (the Chinese Journal of Aeronautics summary returned HTTP 404 to the fetch tool but HTTP 200 to a direct check); their details are provisional.
Luna 16 values (35 cm depth, 101 g return) come from secondary sources and are not confirmed in a primary document.
Luna 20 depth (250 mm vs one metre or more) and sample mass (30 g vs 55 g) conflict between sources; no reliable values recorded.
Luna 24 drilling depth and sample mass are not stated in the primary NASA record; only the 160 cm core length and 8 mm diameter are recorded.
Apollo drill flight list conflicts: NASA Working on the Moon page lists Apollo 13, 15, 16 and 17; Smithsonian record lists Apollo 15, 16 and 17. Apollo 13 did not land; article uses Apollo 15-17.
Apollo drill museum object mass (13.4 kg) and dimensions are recorded for the Smithsonian object, not verified flight configuration.
PRIME-1 TRIDENT: no drilling depth, sample result or ice measurement from the 2025 flight. Drill depth goal and diameter not stated in the NASA article reviewed.
Chang'e-6 drill depth target (2 m) and drill-versus-scoop mass split rely on secondary reporting; CNSA preliminary total 1,935.3 g is from news reporting, not a primary CNSA document.

No direct image asset URL was verified for any drill. The Smithsonian image-delivery URL requires a query string and was set to null. The ALSJ photo catalogue and NASA image feature pages were checked; no verified direct drill image was found. A search-result reference to NASA photo S72-55064 (Cernan operating the Apollo Lunar Surface Drill) was not confirmed on an official page and is not included.
Several reference URLs were fetched only as search results or returned HTTP 403/404; see per-reference notes. Luna 16 reference URL is the form returned by search and was not opened in full.
Power requirements for the Apollo drill battery, Chang'e-5 and Chang'e-6 drills, and TRIDENT are not publicly specified in the sources reviewed; no values were invented.
